name: Lateral lenticulostriate territory
summary: The lateral lenticulostriate territory is the deep region supplied by the lateral striate arteries that rise from the M1 segment through the anterior perforated substance: the posterior putamen, the lateral globus pallidus, the body of the caudate and the upper part of the capsule's posterior limb and the corona radiata. It is the most important small-vessel territory of the hemisphere: it is the site of the pure motor lacune and of the striatocapsular infarct after MCA embolism, the site of the hypertensive putaminal hemorrhage that is the commonest intracerebral bleed, and it has no collateral supply, so it is the irreversible core of every MCA occlusion.

anatomy.location: Posterior two-thirds of the putamen, the lateral part of the globus pallidus, the body of the caudate, the upper two-thirds of the capsule's posterior limb together with the adjacent corona radiata, between the medial lenticulostriate territory in front, the anterior choroidal territory below and behind in the lower posterior limb, and the insular and cortical MCA territories laterally.

afferents.from: Lateral lenticulostriate arteries from the M1 segment

function: The territory contains the corticospinal and corticobulbar fibers and the thalamocortical sensory fibers of the posterior limb, the motor striatum and the lateral pallidum, so its infarction produces the classic capsular syndrome of contralateral face-arm-leg hemiparesis with or without sensory loss, dysarthria and, from the striatum, later dystonia or chorea; a striatocapsular infarct from transient M1 occlusion adds cortical signs (aphasia, neglect) from the hypoperfused convexity. The lateral striate arteries are end-arteries under the direct pressure of the M1 segment, which is why chronic hypertension causes lipohyalinosis and lacunes here and why their rupture produces the putaminal hemorrhage that dissects into the capsule and the ventricle.

bestView.label: lateral lenticulostriate territory of the putamen and posterior limb
lateral striate domain of the lentiform nucleus and internal capsule

imaging.normalAppearance: On the overlay the lateral lenticulostriate domain covers the posterior putamen, lateral pallidum and upper posterior limb; on imaging the lentiform nucleus is the first deep structure to lose density in an MCA occlusion.

pathology.finding: Hyperdense hematoma in the putamen extending into the internal capsule and sometimes the ventricle, with contralateral hemiplegia, gaze deviation and drowsiness.
Comma-shaped restricted diffusion of the putamen, caudate body and capsule with hemiparesis and cortical signs from convexity hypoperfusion.
Small restricted diffusion in the posterior limb with face-arm-leg weakness and no cortical signs.

lesionEffects.deficit: Coma and herniation with large putaminal hemorrhage

examination: Strength of face, arm and leg and the pattern of weakness
Sensation and cortical signs to distinguish a lacune from a striatocapsular infarct
pearls: The lateral lenticulostriates take the full pressure of the M1 and pay for it with lacunes and hemorrhages
Face-arm-leg weakness without cortical signs is the posterior limb
The lentiform nucleus is the core of the MCA stroke: it dies first and does not come back
